before.approach: From the paved pullout at Rainy Pass (4,855 ft) on SR-20 — signed 'Rainy Pass Trailhead,' 52 miles east of Marblemount, right where the PCT crosses the highway — start on the Lake Ann/Maple Pass Trail (well-graded, heavily used). At roughly 1.5 miles, stay right at the Lake Ann junction (the lake itself, just below the junction, is the last reliable on-trail water source) and continue climbing switchbacks through heather meadows to Heather Pass (~6,080 ft, about 2 miles in), where Corteo's east/southeast face comes into full view across the basin. Leave the maintained trail here and traverse climber's-left (south) below Horsefly Pass, holding around 6,400 ft across a broad talus and scree basin beneath the face. Pick a rising traverse line across scree benches and a scree ramp that threads between two low cliff bands to gain Corteo's southeast ridge at about 7,000 ft. From the ridge, work climber's-left up ledges and short rock steps toward a notch at roughly 7,900-7,920 ft just east of the summit block, then finish through blocky class 3 terrain (some parties rope up for a few class 4 moves near the top) to the 8,107 ft summit. All-in, the approach from the trailhead to the base of the face is about 4-5 miles with roughly 2,500 ft of gain to reach the 7,000 ft ridge. Underfoot is loose, downsloping talus and scree for most of the off-trail traverse — a helmet is worth carrying, since the east face sheds rock, especially as the day warms. Snow can linger in the Horsefly Pass basin and across the traverse well into July, so an axe (and possibly crampons) is worth having for early-season attempts.
before.beta: This is Corteo Peak's easiest and most commonly climbed line. After significant off-trail travel from the Maple Pass Loop trail, the route crosses the southeast ridge near 6,900 ft, traverses the south slopes, and gains the southwest ridge around 7,400 ft; from there it follows the ridge crest — sustained class 3 scrambling with real exposure in places and some loose rock — to the 8,107 ft summit. A more technical alternate approach (Lewis Glacier to a notch in the northwest ridge, then the west basin) reaches the same southwest ridge with class 2-4 terrain and a short roped/protected section, but the Maple/Heather Pass line described here is the standard way up.
before.overview: Corteo Peak (8,107 ft) is a double-summited peak on the eastern boundary of North Cascades National Park, 1.7 mi southeast of Black Peak (8,970 ft), rising above the Heather-Maple Pass trail corridor near Rainy Pass. It was first climbed in July 1935 by John Lehmann and Hermann Ulrichs. Two routes are documented: the Southwest Ridge (the standard/easiest line, Class 3-4 scrambling reached via the Lewis Glacier basin, crossing the peak's southeast ridge/basin en route) and a shorter but harder East Face. Corteo is frequently combined with Black Peak in the same trip since both share the Lewis Glacier approach.

climbing_route.label: Southeast ridge to the notch
climbing_route.notes: From the ridge, gained at about 7,000 ft, work climber's-left up ledges and short rock steps toward a notch at roughly 7,900-7,920 ft just east of the summit block. The east face sheds rock, especially as the day warms, so a helmet is worth carrying; snow can linger across the traverse well into July, so an axe (and possibly crampons) is worth having for early-season attempts.

climbing_route.label: Summit block finish
climbing_route.notes: Finish through blocky class 3 terrain to the 8,107 ft summit; some parties rope up for a few class 4 moves near the top.

pitch_detail.notes: Crest of the southwest ridge from roughly 7,400 ft (where the ridge is gained after the southeast-ridge crossing and south-slope traverse) to the 8,107 ft summit; exposed in spots with loose rock underfoot.

itinerary.cal: Best climbed roughly June-August while the Lewis Glacier still holds enough snow for an easy crossing before it softens or thins to bare ice/rock; SR-20 (North Cascades Highway) is gated by snow in winter and typically doesn't open until spring.

days.note: From the Rainy Pass/Maple Pass trailhead, follow the Maple Pass/Heather Pass trail up to Heather Pass, then drop off-trail on snow/talus into the Lewis Lake basin. Most parties camp on a larch bench above the lake to set up for an early glacier start the next morning.
days.title: Approach to high camp above Lewis Lake
days.objective: Reach the larch-bench camp above Lewis Lake

days.note: Leave camp early to cross the Lewis Glacier while it's still firm, gain the ridge notch at about 7,500 ft, down-climb into the West Face cirque, then scramble (exposed Class 3, occasional Class 4) to the summit. Reverse the route back to camp, break camp, and hike out the same day for a long but standard single overnight trip.
days.title: Lewis Glacier, summit push, and hike out

schedule.label: Leave high camp

schedule.label: Down-climb ~400 ft into the West Face cirque

days.objective: Climb the Southeast Face/Southwest Ridge to the summit, then descend and hike out to the trailhead

itinerary.totalNote: A classic one-night trip: ~11 miles and 5,100 ft gain/loss round trip, with an easy approach afternoon followed by a long (~11 hr) summit-and-hike-out day; strong parties can also do it car-to-car in a single 10-13 hr push.

weather.typical: High alpine climate near the crest with snow lingering late into the season
weather.probability: Afternoon thunderstorms are common in mid-summer

seasonal_hazards.exposure: High consequence - sustained exposed, unroped scrambling on loose granite and rhyolite; loose blocks on the face and exposed scrambling, and parties describe a crux narrow ledge with extreme exposure where a slip would likely be very serious

avalanche.zone: N/A - non-glaciated summer scramble route; the nearest NWAC zone (Washington Pass/East Slopes North) only issues forecasts roughly Nov-Apr and does not cover this Jul-Sep climbing window

seasonal_hazards.crevasses: The ascent line on the southeast face itself is not glaciated, but the standard descent via the Southwest Ridge passes the Lewis Glacier remnant/moraine; the glacier is much diminished today but early-season crevasse and icy-margin hazard can still require a rope or crampons/axe.

before.descent_text: The standard descent reverses the same Southwest Ridge line used on ascent, down into the west-face cirque. From the summit, downclimb blocky, exposed class 3 (with a few class 4 moves) south/southwest along the ridge crest to a large notch roughly a third of the way down (approximately 7,600-7,700 ft), reached through an easy connecting gully. That gully has one distinctly steeper step, which is the crux of the way down: most parties downclimb it as class 4 on solid holds, but it is commonly protected with a single-strand rappel (one 30 m rope is sufficient) off natural gear — horns, chockstones, or a sling around a block; no fixed or bolted anchor has been reported here, so carry a few slings/cord. Treat this as optional but be ready for it, especially if the rock is wet or the party is not comfortable down-climbing exposed class 4. Below the step, follow the gully and talus down into the west-face cirque near the Lewis Glacier's east moraine (~6,400 ft), then pick up talus and intermittent boot path south past Lewis Lake to rejoin the trail near Heather Pass. From Heather Pass it's about 2 miles of maintained trail back down to the Rainy Pass Trailhead. This line trades the southeast face's rockfall exposure for glacier/snowfield travel past the Lewis Glacier remnant — rope up or use an axe/crampons if it's icy — and the Horsefly Pass basin can hold avalanche-prone snow into early summer. Total descent is roughly 5-6 miles with about 3,700 ft of net loss back to the car.

approach_variants.name: Rainy Pass and the Lake Ann/Maple Pass Trail to Heather Pass, then the 6,400 ft traverse and the scree ramp between two cliff bands
approach_variants.notes: From the paved pullout at Rainy Pass at 4,855 ft on SR-20, signed Rainy Pass Trailhead, 52 miles east of Marblemount and right where the PCT crosses the highway, start on the Lake Ann and Maple Pass Trail, well-graded and heavily used. AGAIN, THIS IS THE RAINY PASS LAKE ANN, NOT THE ONE BELOW MOUNT SHUKSAN. At roughly 1.5 miles, STAY RIGHT at the Lake Ann junction; the lake itself, just below the junction, IS THE LAST RELIABLE ON-TRAIL WATER SOURCE. Continue climbing switchbacks through heather meadows to Heather Pass at about 6,080 ft, roughly 2 miles in, WHERE CORTEO'S EAST AND SOUTHEAST FACE COMES INTO FULL VIEW ACROSS THE BASIN. Leave the maintained trail there. About 4-5 miles and 2,500 ft of gain from the trailhead to reach the 7,000 ft ridge.
hazards: Loose, downsloping talus and scree for most of the off-trail traverse
The east face sheds rock as the day warms; cross the basin early and carry a helmet
Snow can linger in the Horsefly Pass basin and across the traverse well into July
One distinctly steeper class 4 step on the descent, with no fixed anchor reported
Glacier and snowfield travel past the Lewis Glacier remnant on the descent
Lake Ann is the last reliable on-trail water
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE TRAVERSE IS HELD AT A HEIGHT AND THE ENTRY TO THE RIDGE IS A RAMP BETWEEN TWO CLIFF BANDS, WHICH IS THE ONE DETAIL THAT MAKES THIS FINDABLE. From Heather Pass, traverse climber's-LEFT, south, BELOW HORSEFLY PASS, HOLDING AROUND 6,400 FT across a broad talus and scree basin beneath the face. Then pick a rising traverse across scree benches and A SCREE RAMP THAT THREADS BETWEEN TWO LOW CLIFF BANDS to gain Corteo's southeast ridge AT ABOUT 7,000 FT.

SO THERE ARE TWO NUMBERS AND ONE SHAPE: HOLD 6,400 FT ACROSS THE BASIN, FIND A RAMP BETWEEN TWO CLIFF BANDS, AND GAIN THE RIDGE AT 7,000 FT. In cloud the altimeter does most of the work and the ramp is the only thing you have to see.

IF YOU CANNOT FIND A WAY THROUGH THE CLIFF BANDS, YOU ARE NOT AT THE RAMP. There is one threading line; forcing a cliff band elsewhere is how this approach goes wrong.

FROM THE RIDGE, work climber's-LEFT up ledges and short rock steps toward A NOTCH AT ROUGHLY 7,900-7,920 FT JUST EAST OF THE SUMMIT BLOCK, then finish through blocky class 3 terrain, with some parties roping up for a few class 4 moves near the top, to the 8,107 ft summit.

SO THE SEQUENCE OF HEIGHTS IS 6,400, 7,000, 7,900, 8,107, AND EACH ONE IS A CHANGE OF GROUND: basin traverse, ridge gained, notch, summit block.

A HAZARD THAT IS ALSO A TIMING INSTRUCTION: underfoot is loose, downsloping talus and scree for most of the off-trail traverse, AND THE EAST FACE SHEDS ROCK ESPECIALLY AS THE DAY WARMS. Cross the basin early.

THE DESCENT USES DIFFERENT GROUND FROM THE ASCENT AND THAT IS WORTH PLANNING FOR: it drops southwest along the ridge crest to a large notch roughly a third of the way down at about 7,600-7,700 ft, reached through an easy connecting gully with ONE DISTINCTLY STEEPER STEP, commonly protected with a single-strand rappel on one 30 m rope off natural gear since no fixed anchor has been reported. Below the step, the gully and talus lead into the west-face cirque near the Lewis Glacier's east moraine at about 6,400 ft, then talus and intermittent boot path south past Lewis Lake rejoin the trail near Heather Pass.

fitnessSpec.hiking: 8-10+ mile round trip with roughly 4,000+ ft of gain, full 10-12 hour car-to-car day via Rainy Pass/Maple Pass approach
fitnessSpec.packWeight: light day-climb pack, ~15-25 lbs (no glacier or overnight gear required)

partner_requirements.approachTime: roughly 2-3 hours from the Maple Pass trailhead to the base of the southeast ridge/face before technical scrambling begins
requiredSkills: composure on sustained, exposed narrow ledges ('goat ledge'-style terrain)
judging loose rock and handholds on granite and shattered rhyolite
basic snow travel/self-arrest for lingering early-season snow on the approach and face
partner_requirements.experienceLevel: Intermediate scrambler/alpine climber comfortable soloing exposed Class 4 terrain and short 5.2 moves on loose rock; commonly used as a club 'Basic Alpine Climb' objective, so a solid Basic-level scrambler is appropriate, not a first-timer

access.fees: None — no climbing permit fee (this is National Forest, not Mount Rainier NP)
access.notes: Not inside North Cascades National Park — this corridor is entirely Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest (Methow Valley Ranger District). No Mount Rainier-style climbing fee applies here.
access.rules: Leave No Trace; day travel on the National Forest land near the trailhead needs no permit, but most of the route (Lewis Glacier basin, ridge, and summit) lies within North Cascades National Park/Stephen Mather Wilderness, where overnight camping requires a backcountry permit.
access.permit: Overnight backcountry camping in North Cascades National Park costs $10/person plus a $6 non-refundable reservation fee (charged mid-May-early Oct; free the rest of the year, per the NPS fee schedule updated in 2024). About 60% of permits are reservable in advance on recreation.gov; 40% are held for in-person walk-up at the Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount. Day climbs with no overnight camping do not require an NCNP permit.
access.closures: SR 20 (North Cascades Highway) closes for winter between the Ross Dam Trailhead (MP 134, west) and the Silver Star Gate (MP 171, east), typically mid-November through late April/early May; the exact reopening date varies year to year with snowpack and slide/storm damage, so check the WSDOT mountain pass report before driving.
access.seasonal: WA-20 (North Cascades Highway) closes gate-to-gate roughly early December–mid/late April; the entire Washington Pass corridor is car-inaccessible in winter.
access.landManager: North Cascades National Park Complex/Stephen Mather Wilderness (upper peak and glacier basin); Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, Methow Valley Ranger District (Rainy Pass trailhead and lower trail).
access.land_manager: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest (Methow Valley Ranger District)
access.parking_pass: Northwest Forest Pass required at Washington Pass Overlook, Blue Lake, and Cutthroat trailheads — $5/day or $30/annual (America the Beautiful pass also honored).
access.passRequired: Northwest Forest Pass ($30/yr or $5/day) or an America the Beautiful Interagency Pass to park at the Rainy Pass/Lake Ann Trailhead.

overnight_permit.what: No overnight permit required at Wing or Lewis Lake
overnight_permit.where: These camps are on national forest land outside the park; a Northwest Forest Pass is needed to park at Rainy Pass. Camping inside the park boundary needs a park wilderness permit.

approach_logistics.trailheadDirection: From the paved pullout at Rainy Pass (4,855 ft) on SR-20 — signed 'Rainy Pass Trailhead,' 52 miles east of Marblemount, right where the PCT crosses the highway — start on the Lake Ann/Maple Pass Trail (well-graded, heavily used).

waypoints.name: Rainy Pass / Lake Ann–Maple Pass Trailhead (Trail #740)
waypoints.note: South side of SR 20 at Rainy Pass, ~40-car lot with privy; Northwest Forest Pass required to park.
waypoints.directions: Drive SR-20 to Rainy Pass, about 52 miles east of Marblemount, and turn into the paved lot on the south side of the highway where the PCT crosses. Start on the Lake Ann/Maple Pass trail, which is well graded and heavily used the whole way to the pass.

waypoints.name: Lake Ann Trail junction
waypoints.note: Trail forks here — Lake Ann is 0.3 mi east while the Heather–Maple Pass Trail keeps climbing north/west toward Heather Pass.
waypoints.directions: A bit over a mile of gentle forest climbing brings you to the fork. Stay right on the Heather-Maple Pass trail; the left branch is the short spur down to the lake, which is worth the detour only because it is the last reliable on-trail water — fill here.

waypoints.name: Heather Pass
waypoints.note: High point of the maintained trail; leave the trail here and drop west off-trail toward Lewis Lake — can hold snow into July.
waypoints.directions: Two more miles of switchbacks through open heather meadow above the Lake Ann basin. This stretch faces north and holds snow later than the trail below it, so an ice axe earns its weight in June and early July when the tread disappears under snowfields.

waypoints.name: Lewis Lake larch bench
waypoints.note: Established camp on the larch bench above the lake's south shore; reliable water, but goats here are salt-habituated and bold around packs.
waypoints.directions: Leave the maintained trail at the pass and drop west off the far side on talus and lingering snow, then work around the south side of Lewis Lake to the larch bench above the shore. There is no maintained tread here, but a boot path is usually visible.

waypoints.name: Lewis Glacier / east moraine crossing
waypoints.note: Crampon up snow/glacier remnants on Corteo's north flank to the glacier's east lateral moraine; the glacier is retreating fast and late-season crevasse/moat gaps can open.
waypoints.directions: From the bench continue west across talus and snow, picking up the boot path onto the crest of the glacier's east lateral moraine near 6,400 ft. Early season this is a clean snow slope; by late summer expect bare ice, more exposed rock than the older descriptions imply, and moats where the snow has pulled back from the moraine.

waypoints.name: ~7,500 ft notch atop the moraine
waypoints.note: Gain the ridge crest here and traverse west toward a second notch; narrow, sand-covered ledges with exposure on this stretch.
waypoints.directions: Follow the moraine crest onto the snow and climb southeast, bearing left near the top to reach the notch on the ridge at about 7,500 ft. This is the decision point of the route: bearing right instead of left leads onto narrow, sand-covered ledges with severe exposure and a steep, constricted snow gully above — a substantially harder line that parties have ended up on by mistake.

waypoints.name: Second notch / cirque downclimb
waypoints.note: Downclimb from the second notch into Corteo's west-facing cirque below the Southwest Ridge; loose rock underfoot, stay alert for parties below.
waypoints.directions: From the first notch follow the ridge crest west to a second notch, then downclimb roughly 400 ft of dirt or snow into the cirque under the peak's west face. The ground is loose enough that anything dislodged runs the full length of the downclimb, so space the party out or move one at a time.

waypoints.name: Corteo Peak summit
waypoints.note: True summit (8,107 ft) topped via Class 3-4 scrambling up the Southwest Ridge; views across Ragged Ridge to Black Peak and Buckner.
waypoints.directions: Cross the cirque and climb the southwest ridge to the top on blocky Class 3 with a few Class 4 moves and real exposure in places; some parties put the rope on for the last section. Fix the notch you came down in your mind before you start up — the descent reverses this line and the notch is easy to lose from above.
